description: Hand-labeled test set for evaluating check_compliance() against real German health-advertising law (HWG, UWG). Ground truth labels are derived from the actual ingested legal text, not general knowledge. Verdict scale: 0=fully compliant, 1=compliant with a minor stylistic note (no legal risk), 2=grey area (genuinely ambiguous under the retrieved legal text, needs human legal review), 3=not compliant. Originally a binary compliant/non-compliant set (30 examples); relabeled to the 4-level scale and extended with 3 dedicated grey-area examples (031-033), since none of the original examples were genuinely ambiguous under the law — they were either clear violations or clearly clean.

categories.blocklist: Should be caught by the layer-1 regex blocklist alone (positive control). Always verdict 3.
categories.rag_subtle: Dodges the blocklist but violates a specific HWG/UWG provision, or is a clear guarantee/claim caught by grounded reasoning. Always verdict 3.
categories.minor_note: Compliant but with hyperbolic/puffery language worth a stylistic note — no legal risk. Verdict 1.
categories.grey_area: Genuinely ambiguous under the retrieved legal text — a reasonable case exists for more than one verdict. Verdict 2.

examples.claim: This serum cures acne in just 7 days!
examples.rationale: Contains 'cures acne' — direct cure claim, blocklisted and forbidden under HWG §3 (Irreführungsverbot).

examples.claim: Clinically proven to eliminate wrinkles overnight.
examples.rationale: Contains 'clinically proven' — unsubstantiated clinical authority claim, blocklisted.

examples.claim: Dermatologist approved, guaranteed results with no side effects.
examples.rationale: Multiple blocklist hits: 'dermatologist approved', 'guaranteed results', 'no side effects'.

examples.claim: 100% effective, works every time.
examples.rationale: Contains '100% effective' and 'works every time' — guarantee language, blocklisted.

examples.claim: This is a permanent solution — forever clear skin.
examples.rationale: Contains 'permanent solution' and 'forever clear' — exaggerated before/after language, blocklisted.

examples.claim: My dermatologist friend Julia recommends this brand to all her patients.
examples.rationale: Recommendation from a health professional used in advertising outside professional circles — HWG §11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2. No blocklist phrase match.

examples.claim: As seen on TV and loved by celebrities everywhere — the product everyone's talking about.
examples.rationale: Celebrity-driven recommendation encouraging use based on fame — HWG §11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2.

examples.claim: Look at this insane before and after — I couldn't believe the difference after one week.
examples.rationale: Before/after depiction in a manner likely to mislead about typical results — HWG §11 Abs. 1 Nr. 3/5.

examples.claim: If you don't use this, your skin will only get worse — but with it, you'll glow.
examples.rationale: Generalizes into a promotional promise/threat about what will happen to the reader — HWG §11 Abs. 1 Nr. 7. (Distinct from a personal testimonial, which this is not.)

examples.claim: Use code JULIA20 for 20% off — swipe up! (no ad disclosure shown anywhere in the post)
examples.rationale: Undisclosed commercial intent in a promotional post — a bright-line UWG §5a Abs. 4 violation (failure to disclose commercial purpose), not ambiguous.

examples.claim: This natural remedy works exactly like prescription retinoids, without the hassle.
examples.rationale: Claims equivalent effect to another treatment outside professional circles — HWG §11 Abs. 2.

examples.claim: After using this for two weeks my eczema was completely gone and never came back.
examples.rationale: Direct claim of curing a medical condition — misleading effect claim under HWG §3, advertised outside professional circles.

examples.claim: This product will definitely fix your acne, I promise.
examples.rationale: Implies certainty of effect without the exact blocklisted phrases — misleading guarantee under HWG §3.

examples.claim: There's really no reason to book a dermatologist appointment when you have this in your routine.
examples.rationale: Paraphrase of 'no need for a dermatologist' that avoids the exact blocklisted phrase — tests whether RAG grounding catches rewordings the blocklist misses.

examples.claim: I finally found something that treats my rosacea.
examples.rationale: Direct medical condition treatment claim made outside professional circles — HWG §3 / §11.

examples.claim: Trust me, this WILL work for you.
examples.rationale: Direct guaranteed-outcome promise to the reader, no blocklisted phrasing — misleading guarantee under HWG §3.

examples.claim: I've been using this serum for a month and my skin feels really soft.
examples.rationale: Personal, subjective experience with no medical or guarantee claims.

examples.claim: This is my honest review after 6 weeks of use — results vary by skin type.
examples.rationale: Explicitly hedges on individual variation; no guarantee or medical claim.

examples.claim: I like how lightweight this moisturizer feels under makeup.
examples.rationale: Purely sensory/cosmetic observation, no efficacy or medical claim.

examples.claim: Ad: paid partnership with Formel Skin. Use code JULIA20 for a discount.
examples.rationale: Commercial intent is explicitly disclosed ('Ad:', 'paid partnership') — satisfies UWG §5a Abs. 4.

examples.claim: Everyone's skin is different, so I'd recommend chatting with your dermatologist before trying prescription treatments.
examples.rationale: Directs the audience toward professional medical advice rather than replacing it.

examples.claim: This packaging is so cute, I love unboxing new skincare.
examples.rationale: Aesthetic commentary unrelated to product efficacy.

examples.claim: I read the ingredient list and I like that it has niacinamide.
examples.rationale: Factual ingredient mention, no efficacy or medical claim attached.

examples.claim: Not sponsored, just genuinely enjoy this product.
examples.rationale: Discloses lack of commercial relationship; no problematic claims.

examples.claim: My skin texture has visibly improved since I started this routine two months ago.
examples.rationale: Personal, time-bound, hedged observation without hyperbole or guarantee language.

examples.claim: This is part of a paid collaboration with the brand — as always, opinions are my own.
examples.rationale: Clear commercial disclosure satisfying UWG §5a Abs. 4.

examples.claim: Some people notice a difference in a few days, results vary.
examples.rationale: Explicitly hedges with 'results vary' — no guarantee.

examples.claim: This brand donates part of proceeds to skin health charities.
examples.rationale: Corporate social responsibility statement, unrelated to product efficacy claims.

examples.claim: This brand completely changed my skincare routine.
examples.rationale: Vague marketing puffery ('completely changed') about routine change, not a specific medical or efficacy claim — no legal risk, but the superlative is worth tightening stylistically.

examples.claim: It's basically magic for dry skin.
examples.rationale: Hyperbole ('magic') without a specific medical claim or guarantee — no legal risk, but the word choice could imply exaggerated efficacy and is worth softening.

examples.claim: This gave my skin the reset it needed.
examples.rationale: Genuinely ambiguous: 'reset' could describe a casual subjective impression, or could imply a restorative/therapeutic health effect. The retrieved legal text does not clearly resolve which reading applies — a case for legal review, not an auto-decision.

examples.claim: I feel like my skin finally found balance with this in my routine.
examples.rationale: 'Balance' is ambiguous between a cosmetic/sensory description and an implied physiological claim (e.g. sebum balance), which would be a health-adjacent efficacy claim. Not clearly resolved by the available legal text.

examples.claim: This really evened things out for me.
examples.rationale: 'Evened out' is genuinely ambiguous between describing skin tone (cosmetic) and treating an underlying condition (medical/therapeutic). Warrants human review rather than an automated call.
